newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, bonds rebound; oil soars after attack on Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, bonds rebound; oil soars after attack on Iraq.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks and bonds rebounded from a selloff to end firmer Tuesday, boosted by the shares of oil companies after U.S. military strikes on Iraqi targets lifted oil prices to four-month highs.
The dollar rose broadly as news of American military intervention in Iraq and talk of an imminent rise in U.S. interest rates fuelled demand for the U.S. currency.
American financial markets were closed Monday for the Labour Day holiday.

The Dow Jones industrial average ended up 32.18 points at 5,648.39 after being down more than 50 points in the first minutes of the session as investors worried about higher interest rates and news of the U.S. action against Iraq.
In the broader market, declining issues led advances 1,392 to 1,015 on trading of 333 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
Analysts warned, however, that the market's recovery masked continued uncertainty about interest rates, noting that most of the Dow index's strength came from oil stocks.
The rebound in stocks began with release of the National Association of Purchasing Management index of manufacturing activity for August.

The index, which rose to 52.6 from 50.2 in July, showed gains in the manufacturing sector but fell short of Wall Street's forecasts for a 52.9 reading, leaving unsettled the timing and magnitude of any future action on interest rates by the Federal Reserve.

"After NAPM, which was generally in line with forecasts, you can still make a case both ways," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp. "It left markets with reason to believe the Fed will move and reason to believe it won't."

Late in the session, stocks were given another boost from a report by Lynch, Jones & Ryan Inc., a firm that tracks the retailing business, that retail sales rose just 0.8 percent in August compared to July.
The tame growth surprised analysts, who had expected more of a jump due to back-to-school sales.

The news sparked rise in bonds. The 30-year Treasury bond rose nearly three-quarters of a point and its yield, which moves in the opposite direction from the price, slumped to 7.06 percent from 7.12 percent at Friday's close.

Oil stocks were the session's standouts, as oil prices spiked to their highest level since the Gulf War after the U.S. bombed military targets in Iraq in retaliation for weekend attacks on internationally-protected Kurdish zones.
Crude oil for October delivery closed at $23.40 a barrell, up $1.15, on the New York Mercantile Exchange, The price posted a high of $24.25 in early trading.
Heating oil for October delivery closed up 1.95 cents a gallon at 65.07 cents while October gasoline rose 1.35 cents to 62.96 cents a gallon.
The dollar climbed to seven-week highs against the Japanese yen in a brief rally, leaving the greenback at 1.4840 marks and 109.25 yen in late trading, up slightly from 1.4820 and 108.90 on Friday.
Prices gyrated wildly at the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York.

December coffee fell to a two-week low and closed 4.95 cents a pound lower at 113.30 cents after a biweekly government report released on Friday showed a massive build-up of speculative buyers recently just as commercial coffee firms had hedged or sold the market short.
October world sugar futures soared to close up 0.40 cent a pound at 12.18 cents, the highest close since January 1995.

Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index ended 28.5 points lower at 3,855.9, after rallying from a midsession 48-point tumble. In Tokyo, the key 225-share Nikkei average closed up 91.04 points or 0.45 percent to 20,198.15.
